passages.title: Pixel Learns to Shake
sentences: Sam wanted Pixel to learn to shake.
He held out his hand.
"Shake," he said.
Pixel just sat and looked at him.
Sam tried every day for a week.
On Sunday, Pixel lifted his paw.
He put it in Sam's hand.
Sam laughed and gave him a treat.
"Good boy!" he said. "We did it!"

passages.title: The Long Climb
sentences: Maya and her dad hiked the trail to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
The trail was steep and rocky.
After an hour, Maya's legs felt heavy, and she wanted to stop.
"Let's rest for five minutes," said her dad.
They sat on a log and drank some water.
Then Maya stood up and kept going, one step at a time.
At last, they reached the top.
Maya could see the whole island below.
She saw the harbor, the ferry and the roof of her school.
The sea was blue all the way to the sky.
Maya took a deep breath and grinned.
"I climbed all of it," she said.

passages.title: Leo Helps Jai
sentences: A new boy named Jai came to the skate park with a brand new board.
He stepped on it, and the board rolled away without him.
Jai sat on the ground and looked at the board.
Leo rolled over and stopped next to him.
"That happened to me a lot when I started," Leo said.
"Put your front foot here, over the bolts."
"Bend your knees a little, like this."
Jai tried again, and this time he rolled a few feet.
Leo clapped.
"You'll get it," he said. "I'll be here on Saturday too."

passages.title: Ben's First Club Day
sentences: Ben stood outside Room 12 at Harbor Middle School.
It was the first day of robot club, and every face inside was new to him.
His hands were sweaty, and he thought about going home.
Then the door opened, and Priya waved him in.
"We need someone to build the arm," she said. "Want to try?"
She showed him the box of parts and the plan.
At first, Ben's fingers felt clumsy with the tiny screws.
Priya showed him how to use the small screwdriver.
By the end of the hour, the arm could lift a pencil.
Ben and Priya cheered when it worked.
On the way out, Ben asked, "Same time next week?"
Priya nodded. "Same time next week."

passages.title: Sam's Best Saturday
sentences: Sam's favorite kind of Saturday starts early.
He and Grandma Rose take the 8:15 AM train along the coast.
Sam sits by the window with his map and marks each station they pass.
Pixel rides on the floor by his feet.
At the last stop, they walk to the harbor to watch the big boats come in.
Grandma Rose brings two warm rolls from the bakery in a paper bag.
They eat them on a bench by the water.
Sam tells her facts about the trains, and she listens to every one.
On the ride home, Sam counts the bridges.
There are seven of them.
When they get back, Sam feels tired and happy at the same time.
"Same trip next month?" Grandma Rose asks.
Sam nods fast.

passages.title: Camping in the Living Room
sentences: Ana and Ben had a plan for Saturday.
They would camp with their mom at the Story Woods campsite.
Ben had packed his sleeping bag, a flashlight and a deck of cards three days early.
On Friday night, the weather report showed a big storm coming to the island.
There would be strong wind and heavy rain all weekend.
"I'm sorry," said Mom. "It is not safe to camp in a storm like that."
Ben dropped his bag on the floor and frowned.
Ana felt disappointed too, but then she had an idea.
"What if we camp in the living room?" she asked.
Mom smiled and helped them set up the tent between the couch and the window.
That night, the wind was loud, and the rain hit the glass.
Inside the tent, the twins played cards by flashlight and ate popcorn.
Before he fell asleep, Ben said, "This is a pretty good camping trip."
"We can go to Story Woods next month," Mom said. "The campsite will still be there."

passages.title: Leo Keeps the Beat
sentences: For his birthday, Leo got a practice pad and a pair of drumsticks.
A practice pad is a flat rubber circle that drummers hit to train their hands.
It makes a soft tap instead of a loud bang, so his family did not mind the noise.
Leo wanted to join the Harbor Middle School band in the spring.
To try out, he would need to play a steady beat for one whole minute without speeding up.
The first week was harder than he expected.
Every time Leo got excited, his hands moved faster, and the beat got quicker and quicker.
He felt frustrated, and twice he put the sticks away in a drawer.
Then the band teacher showed him a metronome app on her tablet.
A metronome clicks at an even speed, and a drummer plays one hit on each click.
"Start slow," she told him. "Practice for fifteen minutes every day, and only speed up when slow feels easy."
Leo took the sticks out of the drawer and followed her plan, even on days when he wanted to be at the skate park.
He counted out loud, one, two, three, four, and waited for each click before he hit the pad.
After six weeks, he played for the band teacher again.
The beat stayed steady for the whole minute, and she nodded.
"Welcome to the band," she said.
Leo grinned and tapped his sticks together twice.

passages.title: Ana's Chess Match
sentences: On Thursday afternoons, the Harbor Town library holds a chess club in its back room.
Ana had played chess with her brother Ben for a year, and she won most of their games.
So when Maya asked her to play, Ana felt sure that she would win.
Twenty minutes later, Maya slid her queen across the board and said quietly, "Checkmate."
Ana stared at the board in silence.
Her king was completely trapped, with no safe square left to move to.
On the walk home, Ana told Ben that she did not want to go back to chess club.
Ben thought about it for a moment. "You could ask Maya to explain how she beat you," he suggested.
The next Thursday, Ana walked up to Maya's table and asked.
Maya set up the pieces again and showed her the moves that had trapped her king.
"You brought your queen out too early," Maya explained. "I did that for months when I started."
After that, Ana practiced on a chess app for twenty minutes after her homework.
She solved one puzzle each day and wrote every new idea in a small notebook.
A month later, she and Maya played again.
This time, the game lasted almost an hour, and it ended in a draw, with neither player able to win.
Ana and Maya shook hands, and both of them laughed.
"Rematch next Thursday?" asked Maya, and Ana said yes.

passages.title: Maya's Triceratops
sentences: When Maya opened the box from her aunt, she found a model kit of a Triceratops skeleton.
Inside were 214 plastic bones, a tube of glue, a wooden stand and a thick booklet of instructions.
Triceratops was a plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 68 to 66 million years ago, in what is now western North America.
Its name means "three-horned face," because it had two long horns above its eyes and a shorter one on its nose.
Maya planned to build one section every weekend and to finish in six weeks, in time for the school science fair.
The first two weekends went smoothly.
She sorted the bones into labeled cups, then glued together the long tail and the four thick legs.
On the third weekend, she reached the skull, which the booklet called the hardest part of the kit.
The wide frill at the back of the skull was made of five thin pieces that had to line up exactly.
As she pressed the last piece into place, the frill cracked down the middle.
Maya set it down, pushed back her chair and did not touch the model for the rest of the day.
The next morning, she studied the crack more carefully.
She remembered from a library book that real fossil bones are often found broken into many pieces.
Scientists clean each piece, fit the pieces back together and glue them, one careful step at a time.
So Maya did the same thing: she lined up the two halves, added a thin line of glue and held them still for five whole minutes.
When the glue dried, the crack was a fine line that people could only see up close.
She decided not to paint over it.
Maya attached the last rib on the Friday before the fair.
At her table, she set the model next to a card that said, "Built in six weeks. One crack, fixed the way scientists fix real fossils."
Many visitors asked about the crack, and Maya explained how fossils are repaired.
Ms. Ortiz looked at the frill for a long time.
"The crack is my favorite part," she said.

passages.title: Learning to Live in Space
sentences: On the International Space Station, everyday activities like sleeping, eating and exercising work very differently than they do at home.
The station circles Earth about once every 90 minutes, so the crew can see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets in a single day.
Most astronauts stay on board for about six months, which means they must learn a whole new set of daily routines.
Sleeping is one of the first routines that changes.
Because everything floats, astronauts zip themselves into sleeping bags that are tied to the wall of a small cabin, about the size of a closet.
In space there is no real up or down, so sleeping sideways feels the same as sleeping upright.
Eating changes too.
Drinks come in pouches with straws, because water poured from a cup would float away in wobbly drops.
Crews often eat tortillas instead of bread, since bread makes crumbs that drift around the station and can get into machines.
Staying healthy takes daily work.
Without gravity pulling on their bodies, astronauts' bones and muscles slowly become weaker.
To stay strong, they exercise for about two hours every day on a treadmill, an exercise bike and a lifting machine, using straps to hold themselves in place.
Astronauts often say that their first few days on the station feel strange and clumsy.
They bump into walls, let go of pencils that float away, and forget to strap things down.
Little by little, though, the new routines start to feel normal.
When they return to Earth months later, they have to get used to gravity again, and walking can feel wobbly for a while.
Learning a new routine takes time and patience, whether you are in space or at home.
